prompt: A C fragment reads: if (x > 0) printf("A"); printf("B"); with both prints written on separate, equally indented lines. Which of them is controlled by the condition?
optionA: Both, because they are indented together
optionB: Only the first
optionC: Neither, because there are no braces
optionD: Only the second
correctAnswerText: Only the first
explanation: Without braces a conditional governs exactly one statement, which is the first. Indentation is invisible to the compiler, so lining the two up changes nothing about which is controlled.

prompt: A C fragment reads: if (x > 0) { printf("A"); printf("B"); } How many statements are controlled by the condition?
optionA: One, the first only
optionB: None, because braces separate them from the condition
optionC: Two, but only if they are indented
optionD: Two
correctAnswerText: Two
explanation: Braces group statements into one block, and the whole block is what the condition governs. Indentation plays no part in either direction.

prompt: Are braces compulsory after a C conditional?
optionA: No; without them the conditional governs the single statement that follows
optionB: Yes; a conditional without braces does not compile
optionC: Yes, unless the body is on the same line
optionD: No; without them the conditional governs everything until the next blank line
correctAnswerText: No; without them the conditional governs the single statement that follows
explanation: One statement needs no braces, which is precisely why adding a second line later is such a common way to break working code. Blank lines mean nothing to the compiler.

prompt: A C fragment reads: if (x > 0); printf("A"); What does the condition control?
optionA: The print, which runs only when x is positive
optionB: Nothing, and the fragment does not compile
optionC: Nothing; the semicolon is an empty statement and is the whole body
optionD: The print, which runs regardless of x
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the semicolon is an empty statement and is the whole body
explanation: A semicolon on its own is a complete, empty statement, and the conditional takes it as its body. The print then sits outside the conditional and runs every time — legal, silent and almost never what was meant.

prompt: A C fragment reads: while (i < 5); { total += i; i++; } The program never finishes and never prints anything. Why?
optionA: The braces are in the wrong place and the program does not compile
optionB: The semicolon makes the loop body empty, so nothing ever changes i
optionC: The increment is inside the braces and so never runs
optionD: The condition should have used <= rather than <
correctAnswerText: The semicolon makes the loop body empty, so nothing ever changes i
explanation: The loop repeats an empty statement forever, because nothing inside it can make the condition false. The braced block is a separate block that is never reached, which is why nothing prints either.

prompt: In C, is the condition if (3) satisfied?
optionA: No; only the value 1 counts as true
optionB: No; a condition must be a comparison
optionC: It does not compile; 3 is not a condition
optionD: Yes; any value other than zero counts as true
correctAnswerText: Yes; any value other than zero counts as true
explanation: A C condition is a number, and every non-zero value is treated as true. Requiring a comparison is a rule from other languages that C does not impose.

prompt: A variable holds the result of 2 - 6. Used directly as a C condition, is it satisfied?
optionA: Yes; the result is -4, which is not zero, so it counts as true
optionB: No; a negative result counts as false
optionC: No; only a positive result counts as true
optionD: It cannot be used as a condition without a comparison
correctAnswerText: Yes; the result is -4, which is not zero, so it counts as true
explanation: What matters is only whether the value differs from zero, so a negative result satisfies the test. Reading "true" as "positive" is the natural but wrong reading of a numeric condition.

prompt: In C, is the condition if (0) satisfied?
optionA: Yes; zero is a valid value
optionB: No; and the compiler warns about it
optionC: No; zero is the only value that counts as false
optionD: It depends on whether the zero is written or computed
correctAnswerText: No; zero is the only value that counts as false
explanation: Zero is false and everything else is true, whether the zero was written down or produced by a calculation. Nothing warns about it, which is why a computed zero can quietly disable a branch.

prompt: A C fragment reads: int x = 7; if (x > 5) printf("A"); else printf("B"); What is printed?
optionA: B
optionB: A
optionD: Nothing, since the condition is not stored anywhere
correctAnswerText: A
explanation: The comparison produces a non-zero value, so the first branch runs and the second is skipped. A condition does not need to be stored to be acted on.

prompt: Which C loop form always executes its body at least once?
optionA: while
optionB: for
optionC: None of them; every loop tests before running
optionD: do ... while
correctAnswerText: do ... while
explanation: The do form tests after the body, so the body has already run by the time the condition is examined. Both other forms test first and may run zero times.

prompt: A C while loop is reached with its condition already false. How many times does the body run?
optionA: None
optionB: Once, and then the condition is checked
optionC: Once, because a loop always runs its body
optionD: It does not compile
correctAnswerText: None
explanation: A while loop checks before it runs, so a condition false at entry means the body is skipped entirely. Running once regardless is what the do form would do.

prompt: A menu must be shown and then repeated until the user chooses to quit. Which loop form fits most naturally?
optionA: while, because the choice must be tested first
optionB: for, because the number of repetitions is known
optionC: do ... while, because the menu should appear before any choice exists to test
optionD: Any of them; the forms are interchangeable
correctAnswerText: do ... while, because the menu should appear before any choice exists to test
explanation: There is nothing to test until the menu has been shown once, which is exactly the situation the test-after form exists for. A test-first loop would need a value invented before the first display.

prompt: A while loop and a do ... while loop have identical bodies and identical conditions. On what input do they behave differently?
optionA: Input for which the condition never becomes false
optionB: Input for which the condition is false at entry: one runs the body zero times and the other once
optionC: Input for which the body runs many times
optionD: They never behave differently
correctAnswerText: Input for which the condition is false at entry: one runs the body zero times and the other once
explanation: Once the body has run at all, the two forms proceed identically. Their only difference is what happens before the first test, which is visible only when the condition starts out false.

prompt: A C fragment reads: int x = 0; if (x = 5) printf("A"); What happens, and what does x hold afterwards?
optionA: Nothing is printed, and x holds 0
optionB: Nothing is printed, and x holds 5
optionC: The fragment does not compile
optionD: A is printed, and x holds 5
correctAnswerText: A is printed, and x holds 5
explanation: A single equals assigns and then yields the value assigned, which is non-zero and so satisfies the condition. Both effects happen, which is why answering only one of them misses half of what the line does.

prompt: A loop is written as: int n = 3; while (n = 0) { n--; } How many times does the body run, and what does n hold at the end?
optionA: Zero times, and n holds 0
optionB: Three times, and n holds 0
optionC: Zero times, and n holds 3
optionD: Endlessly, because n is set to 0 every time round
correctAnswerText: Zero times, and n holds 0
explanation: The assignment stores 0 in n and yields 0, which is false, so the loop never enters its body. The variable is changed all the same — a comparison would have run the body three times, which is what a single equals silently costs here.

prompt: A C fragment reads: if (a > 0) if (b > 0) printf("X"); else printf("Y"); with the else indented to line up with the first if. Which if does the else belong to?
optionA: The outer one, on a, as the indentation shows
optionB: Both, since neither has braces
optionC: The inner one, on b
optionD: Neither; the fragment does not compile
correctAnswerText: The inner one, on b
explanation: An else attaches to the nearest unmatched if, and indentation has no bearing on it. Lining the else up with the outer if makes the code read as something it is not.

prompt: The same fragment runs with a = -1 and b = 5. What is printed?
optionA: Y, because a is not positive
optionB: Nothing
optionC: X, because b is positive
optionD: Both X and Y
correctAnswerText: Nothing
explanation: The outer condition fails, so everything inside it is skipped — including the else, which belongs to the inner if. A reader who binds the else to the outer if expects Y, which is exactly what the misleading indentation invites.

prompt: A C fragment reads: for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) printf("%d ", i); What is printed?
explanation: The counter starts at 0 and the loop stops before 3, so 0 1 2 appears. Reading the condition as inclusive adds a fourth value that never occurs.

prompt: How many times does the body run in: for (int i = 2; i <= 11; i += 3)?
explanation: The counter takes 2, 5, 8 and 11, and the last of those satisfies the inclusive condition, so the body runs 4 times. With a step other than one the count is not the difference between the bounds, which is where 9 comes from.

prompt: A C fragment reads: for (int i = 10; i > 0; i++) and the program never finishes. The condition and the starting value are both sensible on their own. What is wrong?
optionA: The starting value should be 0
optionB: The condition should be i >= 0
optionC: The step moves away from the bound, so the condition can never become false
optionD: A for loop cannot count downwards
correctAnswerText: The step moves away from the bound, so the condition can never become false
explanation: A counted loop only ends if its step drives the counter toward the bound, and here it drives it away. Both the start and the condition are perfectly reasonable — it is the relationship between the three parts that fails.

prompt: A counter declared outside a loop runs: for (i = 0; i < 4; i++). What does i hold immediately after the loop?
explanation: The loop ends when the condition first fails, which happens once i has reached 4. The last value used inside the body was 3, which is one less.

prompt: A counter declared outside a loop runs: for (i = 1; i <= 6; i += 2). What does i hold immediately after the loop?
explanation: The counter takes 1, 3 and 5 inside the body, and the step then makes it 7, which fails the condition. The bound itself is never reached, because the step passes over it.

prompt: A program uses the counter after the loop to report how many items were processed, and the figure is always one too high. Each item was processed exactly once. What is wrong?
optionA: The counter holds the value that failed the condition, which is one past the last item
optionB: The loop processes one item too many
optionC: The counter should have started at 1
optionD: The counter is being incremented twice per pass
correctAnswerText: The counter holds the value that failed the condition, which is one past the last item
explanation: Every item being processed once rules out an extra pass, so the count is wrong rather than the work. The counter necessarily ends one beyond the last value it used, which is exactly the discrepancy reported.

prompt: A C fragment declares int sum; without assigning it, then adds three values to it in a loop. What does sum hold at the end?
optionA: The sum of the three values
optionB: Zero, because sum was declared
optionC: The three values added to whatever was already in that memory
optionD: Nothing; the program does not compile
correctAnswerText: The three values added to whatever was already in that memory
explanation: Declaring reserves space without clearing it, so the loop adds to rubbish. The program compiles and runs, which is what makes the wrong total so hard to account for.

prompt: A C function sets a running total to zero, then adds each whole number from 1 to 3 inclusive to it, then reports the total. What does it report?
explanation: The values 1, 2 and 3 accumulate to 6. Answering 3 reports the last value added rather than the accumulated result, and 0 reports the starting value.

prompt: A C program sums an array and prints a plausible but wrong total, and prints a different wrong total each time it runs. The array and the loop bounds are correct. What is wrong?
optionA: The total is being initialised inside the loop
optionB: The array is being read one item past its end
optionC: The total is declared with too small a type
optionD: The running total was never initialised, so each run starts from whatever was in that memory
correctAnswerText: The running total was never initialised, so each run starts from whatever was in that memory
explanation: A different answer on each run is the signature of an unset starting value, since the code and the data are identical between runs. Initialising inside the loop would give the same wrong answer every time.

prompt: A break is reached inside the inner of two nested C loops. Where does execution continue?
optionA: Immediately after the inner loop, still inside the outer one
optionB: Immediately after the outer loop
optionC: At the next iteration of the inner loop
optionD: At the start of the outer loop
correctAnswerText: Immediately after the inner loop, still inside the outer one
explanation: A break leaves exactly one enclosing structure, which is the innermost. Skipping one iteration is what a different instruction does, and leaving both loops needs something more than a plain break.

prompt: A search examines each row of a table, and within each row it abandons the row as soon as its second entry has been checked. The table has 3 rows of 4 entries. How many entries are checked?
explanation: Two entries are checked in each row, because the pass that abandons the row has already examined that entry, and all 3 rows are still visited — 6 entries in all. Abandoning a row ends only the inner structure, so the outer traversal continues.

prompt: A search over a two-dimensional array is meant to stop entirely once a value is found, and it keeps searching later rows. The break is present and does execute. What is wrong?
optionA: The break is inside a conditional and never runs
optionB: The break leaves only the inner loop, so the outer loop begins the next row
optionC: The comparison never matches, so the break is not reached
optionD: The break should have been placed after the inner loop
correctAnswerText: The break leaves only the inner loop, so the outer loop begins the next row
explanation: The break executing rules out it being unreached, and later rows still being searched shows only one structure was left. Stopping both needs a flag the outer loop tests, or a return.

prompt: A multi-way selection on a value has a case for 1 and a case for 2, each ending with a break, and no default. The value is 2. Which cases run?
optionA: Only the case for 1
optionB: Both cases, in the order written
optionC: None, because no default is present
optionD: Only the case for 2
correctAnswerText: Only the case for 2
explanation: Execution enters at the matching case, and the break there leaves the structure before any other case is reached. A missing default is not an error; it means only that an unmatched value would do nothing.

prompt: A C fragment reads: int x = 1; switch (x) { case 1: printf("A"); case 2: printf("B"); break; case 3: printf("C"); break; } What is printed?
optionA: A then B
optionB: A
optionC: A, B then C
optionD: B
correctAnswerText: A then B
explanation: Execution enters at the matching case and continues until a break, so the missing break after the first case lets the second run too. It stops at the break before the third.

prompt: A multi-way selection is meant to handle three values separately, and two of them produce the output of the next case as well. The third behaves correctly. What is wrong?
optionA: The values being matched are wrong
optionB: The default case is missing
optionC: The first two cases have no break, so execution continues into the following case
optionD: The cases are written in the wrong order
correctAnswerText: The first two cases have no break, so execution continues into the following case
explanation: One case behaving correctly shows the structure and the matching work, and the other two producing extra output is exactly what falling through the end of a case does. Order does not affect which case is entered.

prompt: A nested C pair prints i then j on each inner pass: for (i = 0; i < 2; i++) for (j = 0; j < 2; j++) printf("%d%d ", i, j); What is printed?
explanation: The inner loop runs fully for each value of i, so the pairs come out in the order 00 01 10 11. Answering 00 11 advances both counters together, which is what treating the pair as a single loop would do.

prompt: An inner counter is declared outside both loops and is not reset at the start of each outer pass. The outer loop runs 3 times and the inner condition is j < 4. The inner body runs 4 times in total rather than 12. Why?
optionA: The outer loop ran only once
optionB: The inner loop breaks on its fourth pass
optionC: The inner bound should have been 12
optionD: The counter kept its value from the first pass, so the inner condition was already false afterwards
correctAnswerText: The counter kept its value from the first pass, so the inner condition was already false afterwards
explanation: A counter left at 4 fails the condition immediately on every later outer pass, so the inner body never runs again. Declaring the counter inside the loop, or resetting it, is what makes the counts multiply.

prompt: A C function loops over an array and contains a return inside the loop body, not inside any conditional. How many items does it examine?
optionA: One; the return ends the function on the first pass
optionB: All of them; the loop finishes first
optionC: All of them; a return inside a loop acts as a break
optionD: None; the return is reached before the loop begins
correctAnswerText: One; the return ends the function on the first pass
explanation: A return leaves the function immediately, so nothing after it runs and no later pass happens. It is stronger than a break, which leaves only the loop.

prompt: A C function is meant to return the largest value in an array. It returns the first value every time. The comparison inside the loop is correct and the loop bounds are correct. What is wrong?
optionA: The comparison is the wrong way round
optionB: The running maximum starts at zero
optionC: The return sits inside the loop body rather than after it
optionD: The loop examines only the first item because of its bounds
correctAnswerText: The return sits inside the loop body rather than after it
explanation: Correct bounds and a correct comparison leave only where the value is handed back. Returning on the first pass gives the first value whatever the rest of the array holds, which is exactly the symptom.

prompt: A C loop is written as: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++); { printf("%d", i); } It compiles, runs, and prints nothing about the loop. What is wrong?
optionA: The loop condition is never true
optionB: The semicolon ends the loop body, so the braced block runs once, outside the loop
optionC: The braces are not allowed after a for statement
optionD: The printf uses the wrong specifier
correctAnswerText: The semicolon ends the loop body, so the braced block runs once, outside the loop
explanation: The loop repeats an empty statement five times and then the block runs once on its own. It is entirely legal, which is why nothing is reported.

prompt: A C loop is meant to run a two-statement body and only the first statement repeats. It compiles cleanly and the two statements are indented identically. What is wrong?
optionA: A semicolon after the condition ended the body
optionB: The second statement is placed before the loop
optionC: The loop condition becomes false after one pass
optionD: There are no braces, so the loop governs only the first statement
correctAnswerText: There are no braces, so the loop governs only the first statement
explanation: Only the first statement repeating points at what the loop governs, and without braces that is exactly one statement. A semicolon after the condition would have made neither statement repeat.

prompt: Three C faults are all silent: a semicolon after a loop condition, missing braces around a two-statement body, and an else bound to the wrong if. What do they have in common, and why is that dangerous?
optionA: Each produces a valid program with a different meaning, so the compiler has nothing to report and the code reads as intended
optionB: Each produces a compiler warning that is easy to ignore
optionC: Each causes the program to stop at run time
optionD: Each is caught by testing the ordinary cases
correctAnswerText: Each produces a valid program with a different meaning, so the compiler has nothing to report and the code reads as intended
explanation: All three are legal C that means something other than what the layout suggests, which is why nothing complains and why reading the code does not reveal them. Testing may not catch them either, since the ordinary case can happen to give the right answer.

prompt: A team adopts a rule that braces are always written, even around a single statement. What does that prevent, and what does it cost?
optionA: It prevents the semicolon fault, and costs nothing
optionB: It prevents nothing, since a single statement needs no braces
optionC: It prevents a later added line from silently falling outside the structure; it costs two lines of text per conditional
optionD: It costs performance, since braces create a block
correctAnswerText: It prevents a later added line from silently falling outside the structure; it costs two lines of text per conditional
explanation: The danger is not the code as first written but the line somebody adds to it later, which joins the block if braces are there and does not if they are not. Braces are free at run time; the cost is purely in text.

prompt: A C program behaves correctly on every test and contains a missing pair of braces around a two-statement conditional body. How can both be true?
optionA: The compiler inserted the braces automatically
optionB: The tests never exercised a case where the second statement should have been skipped
optionC: Missing braces have no effect when the body is short
optionD: The tests are wrong, since the program cannot be correct
correctAnswerText: The tests never exercised a case where the second statement should have been skipped
explanation: The second statement runs unconditionally, which is only visible on input where the condition is false. If every test satisfies the condition, the fault and the correct code behave identically.

prompt: A C fragment declares int total; then runs a for loop whose condition is false at entry, then prints total. It prints a large unrelated number. The loop body is correct. What happened?
optionA: The loop ran once before the condition was checked
optionB: The loop ran and the body produced a wrong total
optionC: The program printed the loop counter rather than the total
optionD: The loop ran zero times, so total kept the rubbish it was declared with
correctAnswerText: The loop ran zero times, so total kept the rubbish it was declared with
explanation: Two facts combine: a test-first loop can run zero times, and a declared variable holds rubbish until assigned. Either alone would be harmless, and together they print a plausible-looking number that came from nowhere.

prompt: A do ... while loop is given input for which its condition is false from the very start. What does it produce?
optionA: One pass of the body, since the condition is tested only afterwards
optionB: No passes, like a while loop
optionC: An error, since the condition was never true
optionD: Endless passes, since the condition was never true
correctAnswerText: One pass of the body, since the condition is tested only afterwards
explanation: The test-after form has already run its body by the time the condition is examined. That single guaranteed pass is the whole difference between the two forms, and it appears only at this boundary.

prompt: A loop summing an array is given an array of size zero. The total was initialised to 0 before the loop. What is printed?
optionA: An unpredictable value, since the loop never ran
optionB: An error, since an array cannot have size zero
optionC: 0, which is correct and needs no special case
optionD: The value of the loop counter
correctAnswerText: 0, which is correct and needs no special case
explanation: The loop runs zero times and the total keeps the value it was given, which is the right answer for summing nothing. The initialisation is what makes the empty case safe — without it the same loop would print rubbish.

prompt: A loop is meant to run a number of times read from input. What should be checked before it runs, and which loop form makes the check more urgent?
optionA: That the count is not zero; the test-first form, which would loop endlessly
optionB: That the count is not zero or negative; the test-after form, which runs once regardless
optionC: Nothing; a loop handles any count correctly
optionD: That the count is not too large; either form is equally affected
correctAnswerText: That the count is not zero or negative; the test-after form, which runs once regardless
explanation: A test-first loop handles a count of zero correctly by running nothing, so it needs no guard for that case. A test-after loop runs once whatever the count says, which is wrong for zero and worse for a negative value.

prompt: Two C loops differ only in that one initialises its accumulator and one does not. On ordinary input they agree. Where do they part company?
optionA: On large input, where the uninitialised one overflows
optionB: On negative input, where the uninitialised one wraps
optionC: Nowhere; the first pass assigns the accumulator either way
optionD: On input that makes the loop run zero times, where one prints its starting value and the other prints rubbish
correctAnswerText: On input that makes the loop run zero times, where one prints its starting value and the other prints rubbish
explanation: Once the loop runs at least once and the accumulator is assigned before being read, the two behave identically — which is why ordinary testing finds nothing. Only zero iterations leave the starting value visible.

prompt: A while loop is rewritten as a do ... while loop with the same body and condition. They agree on every input the program has been given. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; they differ on input for which the condition is false at entry
optionB: Yes; the two forms are interchangeable
optionC: No; they differ whenever the loop runs more than once
optionD: No; they differ on input for which the loop never ends
correctAnswerText: No; they differ on input for which the condition is false at entry
explanation: Every input tested happened to satisfy the condition at least once, which is where the two forms agree. The separating case is the one the testing never produced.

prompt: A chain of else-if branches is rewritten as three separate if statements with the same conditions and bodies. Are the two equivalent?
optionA: Yes; the same conditions select the same branches
optionB: No; separate statements cannot use the same conditions
optionC: No; where two conditions both hold, the chain runs one branch and the separate statements run both
optionD: Yes, provided the conditions are written in the same order
correctAnswerText: No; where two conditions both hold, the chain runs one branch and the separate statements run both
explanation: A chain stops at its first true condition and separate statements each test independently, so the two agree exactly when no two conditions can hold together. With disjoint conditions they are genuinely equivalent, which is what makes this worth checking rather than assuming.

prompt: A for loop is rewritten as a while loop with the initialisation before it and the step at the end of the body. Are they equivalent?
optionA: Yes, in every case
optionB: Yes for an ordinary body, but not if the body contains a continue, which skips the step in the while version
optionC: No; a for loop can never be written as a while loop
optionD: No; the counter is scoped differently, which changes the result
correctAnswerText: Yes for an ordinary body, but not if the body contains a continue, which skips the step in the while version
explanation: The two forms run the same three parts in the same order until something jumps to the next pass. A continue in the for version still performs the step, and in the rewritten version it skips it, which turns a terminating loop into an endless one.

prompt: Two fragments are equivalent for every input. One uses a multi-way selection and one uses a chain of conditionals. On what grounds should the choice be made?
optionA: On the multi-way selection, which is always faster
optionB: On the chain, which is always clearer
optionC: On neither; equivalent fragments are interchangeable in every respect
optionD: On which states the intent more directly, since behaviour no longer separates them
correctAnswerText: On which states the intent more directly, since behaviour no longer separates them
explanation: Equivalence settles correctness and leaves everything else open, so what remains is whether the next reader can see the structure of the decision. Neither form is universally clearer — a multi-way selection suits matching one value, a chain suits ranges.
